blocks.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th e first quarterly National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for FY 2025/26 covers the period from 1st July to 30th September 2025. Th e report has been prepared to comply with Article 228(6) of the Constitution and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit quarterly budget implementation reports to Parliament for the National and County governments.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th e National Government's gross budget for FY 2025/26 is Kshs.4.69 trillion, compared to Kshs.4.37 trillion for FY 2024/25. Th e gross budget comprises Kshs.744.84 billion for ministerial development expenditure, which accounts for 16 per cent of the gross national budget and 29 per cent of the annual gross ministerial budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Recurrent allocation comprised the ministerial recurrent allocation of Kshs.1.80 trillion (38 per cent of the gross national budget) and Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) at Kshs.2.14 trillion (46 per cent of the annual gross national budget).
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: During the reporting period, receipts into the Consolidated Fund totalled Kshs. 1.03 trillion, accounting for 23 per cent of the annual net estimates of Kshs.4.43 trillion, compared to 18 per cent (Kshs.776.89 billion) received in a similar period of FY 2024/25. Th e total amount issued from the Consolidated Fund to MDAs, CFS, and the Equitable Share to County Governments amounts to Kshs.1.02 trillion, representing 23 per cent of the annual net estimates of Kshs.4.43 trillion, compared to 18 per cent (Kshs.771.71 billion) recorded in a similar period of FY 2024/25. Th e exchequer issues comprised Kshs.43.31 billion (11 per cent) for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.366.49 billion (25 per cent) for ministerial recurrent expenditure, Kshs.546.76 billion (26 per cent) to CFS and Kshs.66.13 billion (16 per cent) in equitable share to County governments.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th e national government's total expenditure for FY 2025/26 amounted to Kshs.1.11 trillion, representing 24 per cent of the national government's annual gross estimates of Kshs.4.69 trillion compared to Kshs.823.78 billion (19 per cent) recorded in a similar FY 2024/25 period. Th is expenditure comprises ministerial development expenditure of Kshs.132.65 billion (with an absorption rate of 18 per cent), recurrent ministerial expenditure at Kshs.433.89 billion (absorption rate of 24 per cent) and CFS expenditure at Kshs.545.48 billion (an absorption rate of 25 per cent).
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Development expenditure with the highest spending included Capital Transfers by the MDAs in subsidies, grants, or direct transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) at Kshs.80.76 billion, representing 61 per cent of the gross development spending. Other major development expenditures included Construction and Civil Works at Kshs.32.56 billion and the Construction of Non-residential Buildings at Kshs.8.27 billion, representing 25 per cent and 6 per cent, respectively, of the gross development expenditure.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: A review of the recurrent expenditure shows that Kshs.164.04 billion was spent on Compensation to Employees, representing 38 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure by MDAs and 28 per cent of the revenue collected, which is in line with the requirement in PFM Regulations 26(1) of 2015 that ministerial expenditure should not exceed 35 per cent of the national government's equitable share of the revenue raised nationally. Total Current transfers to other government institutions were Kshs.171.68 billion and subsidies Kshs.16.44 billion, representing 40 per cent and 4 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure, respectively. Other expenses Implementation Status were Kshs.4.96 billion for travel, Kshs.9.20 billion for security operations and Kshs.5.90 billion for school examination invigilation.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: In the first three months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that should be addressed to ensure seamless budget implementation not only in the current financial year but also for posterity. Th ese
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: included the delay in uploading the procurement plan into the IFMIS system by MDAs, the transition from cash to accrual basis of Accounting, using Article 223 of the Constitution to fund government programmes and Public debt management.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends that the Accounting Officers expedite the implementation of e-GPS as per the Circular by PPRA, in compliance with the Public Procurement and Disposal Act, Cap 412C (the Act), and directives issued by the National Treasury. Th is will ensure transparency, equity, and cost-effectiveness in the use of public resources, as well as the timely implementation of planned activities.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: On the use of Article 223 of the Constitution, the Controller of Budget recommends adopting good planning, budget practices and sound expenditure management by prioritising all essential services and aligning them with operational realities during budget formulation and implementation.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: To enhance fiscal impact and ensure debt sustainability, borrowing should be strictly aligned with development projects that have measurable economic and social returns. Recurrent expenditure should be contained through expenditure rationalisation, efficiency gains, and stronger public financial management controls.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: 1.  INTRODUCTION
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Th is report was prepared in fulfilment of Article 228(6) of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit to each House of Parliament a report on the implementation of the budgets of the national and county governments.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Th is report is in line with Section 9(2) of the Controller of Budget Act Cap 429, which outlines the information to be reported by the Controller of Budget in the quarterly budget implementation reports. To meet the legal requirements governing the content of budget implementation review reports, this report is organised into six chapters. Chapter one is the introduction. Chapter two presents the performance of receipts into the Consolidated Fund and Exchequer Issues to Ministries, Departments and Agencies, Consolidated Fund Services and the County Revenue Fund as part of the equitable share of revenue to the forty-seven counties. Exchequer issues performance is expressed as a percentage of the annual net estimates.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter Th ree presents the overall budget performance of the national government, including performance under the CFS, MDAs' expenditure by economic classification, and the stock of Trade Payables (pending bills) for national government entities.   Chapter Four presents the budget performance of the eighty-seven MDAs clustered into ten Sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, which is planned to support fiscal analysis by breaking down government fiscal statistics for comparability. It presents the approved budget referred to as the gross estimates, actual expenditure, which is further disaggregated into programme and sub-programmes performance and project implementation status for MDAs. Th e absorption rate, which measures the performance, is calculated as a proportion of actual expenditure relative to the annual budget.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: It  is  noteworthy that through Executive Order No. 1 of 2025, repealing Executive Order No. 2 of 2023, the State Department for Performance and Delivery Management was dissolved, and an additional seven State Departments were established. Th ey include the State Department for National Government Coordination, Science Research and Innovation, Public Investments and Assets Management, Special Programmes, Aviation and Aerospace Development, Children Services and Justice, Human Rights and Constitutional Affairs. As a result, the number of MDAs increased from eighty-one in FY 2024/25 to eighty-seven in FY 2025/26.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter Five presents the key issues that were identified as hindering effective budget implementation and provides recommendations to address them. Chapter six provides the conclusion.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Annexes support the chapters. Annex I shows Capital transfer to SAGAs, Annex II details the MDAs' Recurrent Performance by Economic Classification, Annex III shows Current Transfer, Annex IV and V show MDAs' and State Corporations/State Owned Enterprises/SAGAs Trade Payables (pending bills) Annex VI presents the ministerial Development Expenditure; Annex VII details the Recurrent Expenditure, Annex VIII, IX and X shows ministerial development and recurrent expenditure per sector and total expenditure per sector respectively.

blocks.text: 2.1.  Introduction
heading_path: 2.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is chapter presents the receipts into the Consolidated Fund and funds released by the National Treasury in the first three months of FY 2025/2026. Th e funds released went towards funding Consolidated Fund Services, ministerial development expenditure, recurrent expenditure, and transfers to the forty-seven counties.
heading_path: 2.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund
heading_path: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: Th e Consolidated Fund is established under Article 206(1) of the Constitution of Kenya and refers to the account into which all money raised or received by or on behalf of the national government is paid. It excludes monies reasonably exempted by an Act of Parliament and payable into other public funds established for a specific purpose, or is retained by the State organ that received it to defray its expenses. Notably, at the beginning of FY 2023/24, the government directed that all money collected by national government entities as a fee for services offered must be deposited into the e-citizen account, Paybill number 222222.
heading_path: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: To finance the budget, the government, through the National Treasury, targeted to raise funds from various revenue sources. Th e sources include Tax Revenue (Kshs.2.63 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.127.65 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.1.10 trillion - comprising net domestic borrowing of Kshs.634.75 billion and internal debt redemption/roll-over of Kshs.463.51 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.561.81 billion) and other Domestic financing (Kshs.10.80 billion). Th e Government also targeted to raise Kshs.672 billion from Appropriations in Aid (A-I-A) comprising Kshs.334.26 billion recurrent A-I-A and Kshs.337.74 billion development A-I-A.
heading_path: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: 2.2.1  Receipts into the Consolidated Fund
heading_path: 2.2.1  Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

Th e receipts comprised opening balances from the previous financial year (FY 2024/2025), Tax and Non-Tax Revenue, Domestic borrowing, External Loans and Grants, and Other Domestic Financing. blocks.text: 2.4.6  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund
heading_path: 2.4.6  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: Th e Equalisation Fund is established under Article 204 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that half a per cent (0.5 per cent) of all the revenue collected by the National government each year, calculated based on the most recent audited revenue received, as approved by the National Assembly, to be paid into the Fund. Article 204(2) of the Constitution provides that the National Government shall use the Equalisation Fund to provide only essential services, including Water, Roads, Health Facilities, and Electricity to marginalised areas to the extent necessary to bring the quality of those services in those areas to the level generally enjoyed by the rest of the nation, so far as is possible.
heading_path: 2.4.6  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: In  the  first  three  months  of  FY  2025/26,  the  Controller  of  Budget  authorised  three  requests  amounting  to Kshs.116.16 million from the Equalization Fund. Th e amount comprised of, Kshs.68.16 million for Policy 1 development Trade Payables (Pending Bills) in favour of the Ministry of Water and Sanitation and Kshs.48 million for the Second Policy development projects in Samburu County.

blocks.text: 3.1.  Introduction
heading_path: 3.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is chapter presents an overview of the National Government budget implementation in the first three months of FY 2025/26.  It also presents the budget performance of the Consolidated Fund Services (classified as recurrent expenditure), which contains information on Public debt, Pensions and gratuities, Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional officeholders, and Miscellaneous services. Th e chapter further disaggregates expenditure for MDAs under economic classification for ministerial development and recurrent expenditure, respectively.  Additionally, it presents the status of payables as of September 30, 2025 for the national government.
heading_path: 3.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: 3.2.    FY 2025/2026 Overall Budget
heading_path: 3.2.    FY 2025/2026 Overall Budget

blocks.text: Th e approved gross national government budget for FY 2025/26 amounted to Kshs.4.69 trillion, representing 7 per cent growth compared to Kshs.4.37 trillion in FY 2024/2025. Th is comprised of Kshs.744.84 billion for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.1.80 trillion for ministerial recurrent expenditures, and Kshs.2.14 trillion for CFS.  Ministerial development expenditure is to be funded through the net supply (from the government exchequer) of Kshs.407.10 billion and Appropriation-in-Aid (AIA) Kshs.337.74 billion.  Ministerial recurrent expenditure is to be funded by the government through the exchequer, amounting to Kshs.1,470.45 billion and AIA of Kshs.334.26 billion.   In FY 2025/26, the Equitable shareable revenue to County governments amounted to Kshs.415 billion.
heading_path: 3.2.    FY 2025/2026 Overall Budget

blocks.text: To finance the budget, the government targeted to raise funds from various sources. Th e sources include Tax Revenue  (Kshs.2.63  trillion),  Non-Tax  Revenue  (Kshs.127.65  billion),  Domestic  borrowing  (Kshs.1.10  trillion - comprising net domestic borrowing of Kshs.634.75 billion and internal debt redemption/roll-over of Kshs.463.51 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.569.81 billion) and other Domestic financing (Kshs.10.80 billion). Th e Government also targeted to raise Kshs.672 billion from Appropriations in Aid (A-I-A) comprising Kshs.334.26 billion recurrent A-I-A and Kshs.337.74 billion development A-I-A.

blocks.text: 3.3.2  Overdra ft Facility
heading_path: 3.3.2  Overdra ft Facility

blocks.text: Th e overdra ft facility is a way of short-term borrowing by the Government to cover temporary cash shortfalls. It is repayable within twelve months.  Kenya's Government overdra ft is administered through the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK).  It is restricted to a maximum of five percent of the most recently audited revenues and is expected to be paid off by the end of the financial year as specified in Section 15 (3) of the PFM Act.
heading_path: 3.3.2  Overdra ft Facility

blocks.text: In the period under review, the overdra ft limit stood at Kshs.97.05 billion and was charged at an average interest rate of 9.6 per cent per annum on the amount outstanding at the end of each month.  In the first three months of FY 2025/2026, the total charge on the overdra ft facility was Kshs.697.47 million, as shown in Table 3.6.

heading_path: 3.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is section presents an analysis of the MDAs' expenditure by economic classification for the first three months of FY 2025/2026 of both development and recurrent expenditure. Th e development expenditure is disaggregated into major economic items, which include: Capital Transfers to SAGAs, Civil Works and Construction of Residential and Non-Residential Buildings, Refurbishment of Buildings/infrastructure, Purchase of Specialized Plant, Equipment, and Machinery, and Pre-Feasibility studies. blocks.text: 4. BUDGET PERFORMANCE BY SECTOR
heading_path: 4. BUDGET PERFORMANCE BY SECTOR

blocks.text: 4.1.   Introduction
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability. Th e chapter presents the performance of MDAs by sector in the first three months of FY 2025/2026. It provides budget allocations per sector detailing specific MDAs' exchequer issues, expenditures, and absorption on the budget. Th e chapter also presents the performance of MDAs' programmes and sub-programmes and spending on development projects in the first three months of FY 2025/2026.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: Sector performance is presented in alphabetical order as follows; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT), (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (EWNR) (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation (SPCR) Sectors.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: In FY 2025/2026, the Education Sector was allocated Kshs.703.07 billion, recording the highest budget allocation, attributed to its broad mandate, including primary schools, secondary schools, special education, tertiary education, university education, examinations and curriculum development, and reforms in the education sector. Conversely, the General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector received Kshs.58.16 billion, representing the lowest budgetary allocation.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector 4.2.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Agriculture is a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. It is a critical sector in the economic pillar of the Kenya Vision 2030. Th e ARUD Sector comprises five sub-sectors, namely: Th e State Department for Lands and Physical Planning; the State Department for Livestock Development; the State Department for the Blue Economy and Fisheries; the State Department for Agriculture; and the National Land Commission (NLC), together with affiliated Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) and Training Institutions.
heading_path: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector is a significant player in the delivery of national development agendas, namely, Kenya Vision 2030, the government plan -the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (2022-27), the Sustainable Development Goals, and the Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy, among other national and international policies and obligations. During the MTEF period 2025/26-2027/28, the sector plans to implement programmes that facilitate food and nutrition security, agro-processing, employment creation, and the utilisation of the blue economy.
heading_path: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector 4.2.1  Introduction

heading_path: 4.2.3 Th e State Department for Lands and Physical Planning

blocks.text: Th e State Department for Lands and Physical Planning is mandated with national lands policy and management, physical planning for land use, land transactions, survey and mapping, land adjudication, land registration, national spatial infrastructure, land and property valuation services administration, land information systems, maintenance of a public land bank, administration of public land as designated by the Constitution, Land Settlement Policy and Management, Land Settlement Matters and Rural Settlement Planning.

heading_path: 4.2.6 Th e State Department for  the Blue Economy and Fisheries

blocks.text: Th e State Department for the Blue Economy and Fisheries is mandated to coordinate the development of national oceans and blue economy strategies and policies, including Fisheries and Aquaculture Policy, as well as  the  Legal,  Regulatory,  and  Institutional  Framework  for  the  Fisheries  Industry  and  the  Blue  Economy. heading_path: 4.3.  Education Sector

blocks.text: 4.3.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  Education  Sector  comprises  five  MDAs: Th e  State  Department  for  Vocational  and  Technical Training, the State Department for Higher Education, the State Department for Science, Innovation and Research, the State Department for Basic Education and the Teachers Service Commission (TSC) and their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector envisions attaining ' Quality and inclusive education, training and research for sustainable development ' in Kenya. Th e Sector's strategic objectives include enhancing access, equity, quality and relevance in education, training and research; establishing, maintaining and managing professional teaching and learning services for all early learning centres, primary, secondary and tertiary institutions; enhancing development capacities for Science Technology and Innovations; enhance mechanisms for dissemination and commercialisation of research findings; improve data quality and sharing in education, training, research and labour market; promote vibrant industry - institutional linkages in the area of skilling for employability; and integrate ICT in Education, Training and Research for management, teaching and learning at all levels.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: It is worth noting that the ongoing transition from the 8-4-4 to the 2-6-3-3 system requires substantial infrastructure, equipment, and human capital in the medium term, from 2025/26 to 2027/28.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.3.2  Budget Performance for the Education Sector
heading_path: 4.3.2  Budget Performance for the Education Sector

blocks.text: Th e  budgetary  allocation  to  Education  in  FY  2025/2026  amounted  to  Kshs.703.07  billion,  compared  to Kshs.681.98 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. Th is amount represents 15 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 28 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.29.78 billion (4 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.673.29 billion (96 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e Teachers Service Commission received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.387.18 billion (55 per cent of the Education Sector's budget), while the State Department for Science, Innovation and Research had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 0.99 billion (0.1 per cent of the Education Sector allocation).

blocks.text: 4.3.3 Th e State Department for Vocational and Technical Training
heading_path: 4.3.3 Th e State Department for Vocational and Technical Training

blocks.text: Th e mandate of the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training (TVET) is to provide a skilled workforce that supports socio-economic development and fully participates in the global economy. TVET implements key programmes, including institution-based training, apprenticeships, Recognition of Prior Learning, and Entrepreneurship. It improves productivity, competitiveness, and prosperity for individuals, enterprises and the nation.

blocks.text: 4.3.7 Th e Teachers Service Commission
heading_path: 4.3.7 Th e Teachers Service Commission

blocks.text: Th e Teachers Service Commission is mandated to formulate policies that regulate the teaching profession and guide teacher management functions, thereby ensuring compliance with the teaching standards prescribed from time to time, facilitating teachers' career progression and professional development, and monitoring their conduct and performance during curriculum implementation. TSC registers trained teachers and recruits, employs, and assigns teachers employed by the commission. It also exercises disciplinary controls over registered teachers, terminates the employment of teachers, reviews the standards of education and training for persons entering the teaching service, reviews the demand for and supply of teachers, and advises the national government on matters related to the teaching profession.

blocks.text: 4.4.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector 4.4.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.4.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is Sector consists of nine MDAs: Th e State Department for Roads, Transport, Shipping and Maritime Affairs, Housing and Urban Development, Public Works, Information Communications Technology and Digital Economy, Broadcasting and Telecommunications, Energy, and Petroleum.
heading_path: 4.4.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e EIICT sector aims to provide sustainable infrastructure development, a vibrant shipping and maritime industry, universal access to Information Communications Technology (ICT), Transport and built environment services, and accessible, affordable, quality and competitive energy and petroleum products.
heading_path: 4.4.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e EI&ICT Sector plays a vital role as an enabler of the country's socio-economic development. It is a crucial sector in realising Vision 2030 and the BETA Agenda.
heading_path: 4.4.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.4.2  Budget Performance for EIICT Sector
heading_path: 4.4.2  Budget Performance for EIICT Sector

blocks.text: Th e budget allocation to EIICT in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.534.63 billion, compared to the Kshs.444.29 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. Th is amount represents 11 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 21 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs. 380.44 billion (71 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.154.19 billion (29 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Roads received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.221.79 billion (42 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Public Works had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.4.44 billion (0.8 per cent of the EIICT Sector allocation).

heading_path: 4.4.3 Th e State Department for Roads

blocks.text: Th e State Department for Roads promotes the development of national road development policy; develops, standardise and maintains roads; materials testing and advice on usage; protects road reserves; maintains security roads; administers mechanical and transport funds; registration of engineers; provides mechanical and transport services; and enforcement of axle load control. Th e mandate is carried out by the State Department for Roads and its agencies, Th e Kenya Roads Board, Kenya National Highway Authority (KeNHA), Kenya Urban Roads Authority (KURA), Kenya Rural Roads Authority (KeRRA), Engineering Board of Kenya and Kenya Engineering Technology Registration Board.

blocks.text: 4.5.  Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector
heading_path: 4.5.  Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector

blocks.text: 4.5.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources (EPWNR) Sector comprises six MDAs: State Departments for Environment and Climate Change; Forestry; Water and Sanitation; Irrigation; Wildlife; and Mining. Th e sector has several autonomous and semi-autonomous government agencies. In addition, it has the following entities: Th e National Environment Complaint Committee, the National Environment Tribunal, the Hydrologists Registration Board, and the Wildlife Clubs of Kenya.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e goal of the Sector is to ensure sustainable development in a clean and secure environment with various objectives, including enhancing climate change resilience and low carbon emission, improving utilisation of land through irrigation and land reclamation, and promoting equitable and sustainable use of wildlife resources. Th e Sector plays a pivotal role in securing, stewarding, and sustaining the environment, Kenya's natural capital, water provision, and generating foreign exchange for the country.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.5.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector
heading_path: 4.5.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector

blocks.text: Th e budget allocation to the EPWNR Sector in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.95.87 billion, compared to the Kshs.85.37 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. Th is amount represents 2 per cent of the annual gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 4 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Th e allocation comprises Kshs.61.99 billion (65 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.33.88 billion (35 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Water and Sanitation received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.53.95 billion (56 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Mining had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.1.63 billion (2 per cent of the Sector's allocation).

blocks.text: 4.6.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector 4.6.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.6.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) sector consists of eight MDAs, namely the State Departments for Trade; Arid and Semi-arid Lands (ASALs) and Regional Development; Cooperatives; Industry; Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development; Investment Promotion; East African Community; and Tourism together with their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.
heading_path: 4.6.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e objectives of the Sector over the MTEF period are to transform Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), promote and sustain tourism, promote industrial development investments, enhance trade and ease of doing business, promote growth and development of cooperatives and the MSMEs Sector, promote regional integration, and promote equitable and sustainable ASAL and regional development.
heading_path: 4.6.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.6.2  Budget Performance for GECA Sector
heading_path: 4.6.2  Budget Performance for GECA Sector

blocks.text: Th e budget allocation to GECA in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.58.16 billion, compared to Kshs.60.90 billion allocated in FY 2024/20245. Th is amount represents 1 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 2 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.21.60 billion (37 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.36.56 billion (63 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Tourism received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.16.54 billion (28 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for the East African Community had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.1.03 billion (2 per cent of the GECA Sector allocation).

blocks.text: Th e  State  Department  for  Trade  promotes  Trade  Policy;  Export  Development  and  Promotion;  Promote E-Commerce; Trade Negotiations and Advisory Services; Champion Trade Integration in the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), Continental Free Trade Area  (CFTA), Economic Partenership

blocks.text: Agreement (EPA) etc.; Liaising and Coordinating with  (UNCTAD) and World Trade Organisation (WTO) on Trade Matters; Enforcement of International Trade Laws, Negotiations and Agreements; Protection of Kenyan Goods against Dumping and Subsidised Imports and recommending Countervailing Measures; Coordination of multi-Agency Task Force on the Elimination of Illicit Trade and Counterfeits; Liaison with International Trade bodies for National Development; Management of weight and measurement in Trade; Promotion and Regulation of the Wholesale and Retail Trade; and Promotion of Fair-Trade Practices and Consumer Protection. Th e State Department for Trade is assisted by its agencies, including the Kenya National Trading Corporation, the Kenya Export Promotion and Branding Agency, the Warehouse Receipt System Council, the Kenya Trade Remedies Agency, the Kenya Consumer Protection Advisory Committee, and the Kenya National Multi Commodities Exchange Limited.

heading_path: 4.6.4 Th e State Department for the ASALs and Regional Development

blocks.text: Th e State Department for the ASALs and Regional Development promotes Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Policy; Coordination of Planning, and Development for Arid and Semi-Arid Lands; Implementation of Special Programmes for the Development of Arid and Semi-Arid Areas; Implementation of Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Programmes; Coordinating Research for sustainable Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Resource Management, Development and Livelihoods; Promotion of Livestock Development, Marketing and Value addition of Resources within Arid and Semi-Arid Areas; Enhancing Livelihood Resilience of Pastoral and Agro Pastoral Communities; Coordinating Responses Against Drought and Desertification; Special Programmes; Food Relief Management and Humanitarian Emergency Response; Peace Building and Conflict Management within Arid and Semi-Arid Area; Management and Promotion of Integrated Cross-border Activities in Identified ASAL Counties;  Regional  Development Policy Implementation, Oversight and Management; Coordination of Regional Development Authorities; and Projects in Response to Displacement Impacts. heading_path: 4.6.5 Th e State Department for Industry

blocks.text: Th e  State  Department for Industry promotes and facilitates domestic and Foreign Investments; Investment policy and attraction; Industrial Policy and Planning; Buy Kenya - Build Kenya Policy and Strategy; promotes standardisation in Industry and Quality Control; Kenya Property Rights Policy (Patents, Trade Marks, Service Marks, and Innovation); Promotion of Value Addition and Agro Processing; Promotion, Development and Oversight of Aggregation and Industrial Parks; Textile Sector Development; Leather Sector Development and
heading_path: 4.6.5 Th e State Department for Industry

blocks.text: Promotion of Value Chain; Oversight and Regulation of the Scrap Metal Industry; Industrial Training and Capacity Development; To Combat Counterfeiting, Trade and Other Dealings in Counterfeit Goods; and Oversight, Administration and Enforcement of the Local Content Policy. heading_path: 4.6.6 Th e State Department for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development

blocks.text: Th e  State  Department for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises(MSMEs) Development Promotes MSMEs Policy; Develop SME Financing Policy to facilitate adequate flow of credit from financial institutions; Administration of the 'Hustler Fund' for the promotion, development and enhancing competitiveness of MSMES; Capacity Development for Entrepreneurship including access to modern management practices; Support for technology upgradation and modernisation; Establishment of integrated infrastructural facilities; Promotion and  Development of  Micro  and  Small  Enterprise  and  enhance  their  competitiveness;  Promote  Progressive credit policies and practices targeting MSMEs; Business Innovation and Incubation; Administer Preference in Government procurements to products and services of the MSMEs; Champion subcontracting arrangements between SMEs and Large Enterprises; Market development for MSME products and services (better access to domestic and export markets); Support for product development, design intervention and packaging; Promotion of establishment of Production clusters; and Promotion and Development of the Cottage Industry. blocks.text: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector 4.7.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector consists of seventeen MDAs, which include the State Department for Correctional Services; the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services; the National Police Service; the State Department for Internal Security and National Administration; the State Law Office; the Judiciary; the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC); the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP); the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP); the Witness Protection Agency
heading_path: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: (WPA); the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNHCR); the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC); the Judicial Service Commission (JSC); the National Police Service Commission (NPSC); the National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC); the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) and the State Department for Justice, Human Rights and Constitutional Affairs, as well as SAGAs and tribunals each with specific functions and mandates.
heading_path: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  Sector  creates  a  conducive  environment for the country's economic, social, and political development, which is necessary for fulfilling the objectives of Kenya Vision 2030. It comprises institutions with linkages to peace- and security-building, interpretation of the law, correctional services, immigration and population management, legal advisory services to government agencies, representation of the national government in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. Further, the Sector promotes good governance and integrity and spearheads the fight against corruption, public prosecutions, registration and regulation of political parties, protection of witnesses, protection and promotion of human rights, delimitation of electoral boundaries and management of the electoral process, promotion of gender equality, and the inclusion of marginalised groups and communities.
heading_path: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is Sector is also responsible for developing and implementing citizenship and refugee management and immigration services, regulating the gaming industry, providing population management, eradicating drugs and substance abuse, conducting crime research, printing government documents, and overseeing policing.
heading_path: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector
heading_path: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector

blocks.text: Th e budget allocation to GJLO in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.283.04 billion, compared to Kshs.230.89 billion allocated in the financial year 2024/2025. Th is amount represents 6 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 11 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.18.92 billion (7 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.264.12 billion (93 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e  State  Department for National Police Service received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.127.09 billion (50 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.530.33 million (less than 1 per cent of the GJLO Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector

blocks.text: Th e high allocation to the State Department for the National Police Service was due to the provision of security to the government's critical infrastructure and other related activities. blocks.text: 4.8.    Health Sector
heading_path: 4.8.    Health Sector

blocks.text: 4.8.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Health is primarily a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. Th e health sector is responsible for providing and coordinating health policy formulation, ensuring quality service delivery, and regulating health care at the national level. Th e sector comprises two MDAs: Th e State Department for
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Medical Services and the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards. Th e Sector delivers services through several SAGAs and entities, including the Kenyatta National Hospital, Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, Kenya Medical Research Institute, Kenya Medical Supplies Authority, Kenya Medical Training College, National Syndemic Disease Control Council, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research Hospital, National Cancer Institute of Kenya and the Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector envisions 'a healthy, productive and globally competitive nation ' achieved through strategic objectives under equity, efficiency, and people-centred principles with a multi-sectoral approach as outlined in the Kenya Health Policy (2014-2030). Th e Health Sector implements its strategic objectives through eight budgetary programmes, four under the State Department for Medical Services and four under the State Department for Public Health and Professionals.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for the Health Sector
heading_path: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for the Health Sector

blocks.text: Th e budget allocation to the Health Sector in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.138.11 billion, compared to the Kshs.135.19 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. Th is amount represents 3 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 5 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Th e allocation includes Kshs.27.50 billion (20 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.110.61 billion (80 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Medical Services received the highest budget allocation of Kshs.105.95 billion (77 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards was allocated Kshs.32.15 billion (23 per cent of the Health Sector allocation).

blocks.text: Th e  State  Department  for  Public  Health  and  Professional  Standards  promotes  quality  healthcare  services through the provision of policies on healthcare, standards, human resource development, and public health standards and sanitation management. blocks.text: 4.9.   National Security Sector
heading_path: 4.9.   National Security Sector

blocks.text: 4.9.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e National Security sector comprises the Ministry of Defence and the National Intelligence Service (NIS). Th e sector's mandate is to ensure the country's security against any threats emanating from within or outside the Kenyan borders, defend the country, and support the civil powers in maintaining peace and order.
heading_path: 4.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.9.2  Budget Performance for National Security Sector
heading_path: 4.9.2  Budget Performance for National Security Sector

blocks.text: Th e budget for the National Security sector in FY 2025/2026 is Kshs.253.77 billion, compared to Kshs.238.36 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. Th e allocation comprised Kshs.4.93 billion for development expenditure (2 per cent of the sector's budget) and Kshs.248.84 billion for recurrent expenditure (98 per cent of the sector's allocation). Th e Ministry of Defence gross estimates amount to Kshs.202.32 billion (78 per cent of the sector's allocation), while NIS amounts Kshs.51.45 billion (22 per cent of the sector's allocation). Th e growth in the budget allocation for the National Security sector is attributed to increased funding requirements for military modernisation, enhanced territorial defence capabilities, and strengthened intelligence-gathering operations.

blocks.text: 4.9.3 Th e Ministry of Defence
heading_path: 4.9.3 Th e Ministry of Defence

blocks.text: Th e Ministry of Defence encompasses the Kenya Army, Kenya Air Force, Kenya Navy, Defence Forces Constabulary and Civilian Staff. Its primary mandate is to defend and protect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Kenya. Its secondary mandate includes assisting and cooperating with other authorities during emergencies or disasters, and restoring peace in any part of Kenya affected by unrest or instability, as directed. Th e Ministry is committed to defending and protecting the people and property of the Republic of Kenya against external threats and supporting civil authority as per the law.

blocks.text: 4.10.  Public Administration and International Relations Sector
heading_path: 4.10.  Public Administration and International Relations Sector

blocks.text: 4.10.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) sector consists of twenty-three MDAs, namely
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Executive Office of the President, Office of the Deputy President, Office of the Prime Cabinet Secretary, State Department for National Government Coordination, State Department for Parliamentary Affairs, State Department for Cabinet Affairs; State Department for Special Programmes; State House; State Department for Devolution; State Department of Economic Planning; State Department for Foreign Affairs; State Department for Diaspora Affairs; Th e National Treasury; State Department for Public Investments and Assets Management; State Department for Public Service; Parliamentary Service Commission; National Assembly; Parliamentary Joint Services; Senate; Th e Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA); Public Service Commission; Salaries and Remuneration Commission; Th e Auditor General; Th e Controller of Budget and Th e Commission on Administrative Justice (CAJ) together with affiliated SAGAs and entities.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  Sector  provides  national  leadership,  oversight,  and  policy  direction  towards  realising  the  country's  development agenda. It promotes prudent public finance management and accountability in the Public Sector, coordinates national and sectoral development planning, and oversees an efficient and effective Public Service. It also coordinates Kenya's foreign policy and diaspora affairs, wage bill management, development of a sound legislative and regulatory framework, and enforces administrative justice and the right to information.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  sector  has  prioritised  programmes  and  projects  aligned  with  the  Post-COVID-19  Economic  Recovery Stimulus Programme (PC-ERS), the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda, and the Fourth Medium Term Plan of Kenya Vision 2030. Priority was also accorded to ongoing interventions supporting the 'Big Four' agenda and the newly established institutions.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation (SPCR) Sector comprises seven MDAs: the State Departments for Youth Affairs and Creative Economy, Sports, Children Welfare Services, Culture, Th e Arts and Heritage, Labour and Skills Development, Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs, and Gender and Affirmative Action.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e strategic roles played by the Sector in the country's transformation and socio-economic development include Promoting and supporting youth empowerment and development; strengthening youth mainstreaming in  all  sectors;  spearheading  the  management  of  youth  policy  and  legislations;  promoting  engagement  with youth for national development; promotion of sustainable employment, harmonious industrial relations, and productive workforce; promotion of gender equity and equality; empowerment of communities and vulnerable groups, safeguarding children's rights; and advancement of diverse cultures, arts and sports to enhance cohesiveness and Kenya's regional and international competitiveness.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector
heading_path: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector

blocks.text: Th e budget allocation to SPCR in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.78.99 billion, compared to Kshs.83.93 billion allocated in the previous financial year of 2024/2025. Th is amount represents 2 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 3 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Th e allocation comprises Kshs.24.85 billion (31 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.54.15 billion (69 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs received the highest budget-

blocks.text: ary allocation of Kshs.29.32 billion (37 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Culture and Heritage had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.3.59 billion (5 per cent of the SPCR Sector allocation). blocks.text: Th e total exchequer issues to the SPCR Sector amounted to Kshs.17.56 billion, representing 31 per cent of the Sector's annual net estimates, comprising Kshs.2.16 billion for development expenditure, representing 28 per cent of original development net estimates, and Kshs.15.39 billion for recurrent activities, representing 31 per cent of annual recurrent net estimates.
heading_path: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector

blocks.text: In the first three months of FY 2025/2026, the State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs received the highest proportion of recurrent exchequer issues to revised net estimates at 36 per cent, while the State Department for Gender and Affirmative Action received the lowest at 11 per cent. Th e State Department for Gender and Affirmative Action recorded the highest proportion of development exchequer issues to annual development net estimates at 49 per cent, while the State Department for Youth Affairs and Creative Economy recorded the lowest ratio of 1 per cent.

blocks.text: 4.11.6 Th e State Department for Children Services
heading_path: 4.11.6 Th e State Department for Children Services

blocks.text: Th e State Department for Children Services promotes and safeguards the rights and welfare of all children in Kenya. Its role is to provide leadership in coordination, policy implementation, and the delivery of services related to child protection and well-being. Th is includes preventing and responding to issues like child abuse, exploitation, child labour, and harmful practices, as well as managing institutions for children and promoting alternative family care.
heading_path: 4.11.6 Th e State Department for Children Services

blocks.text: Th e budget allocation to the State Department for Children Welfare Services in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.12.32 billion. It was created on 16 th April 2025 following the reorganisation of the government structure.

blocks.text: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS

blocks.text: In the first three months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that should be addressed for seamless budget implementation. Th ese included the delay in uploading the procurement plan into the IFMIS system by MDAs, the transition from cash to an accrual basis of Accounting, using Article 223 of the Constitution to fund government programmes, and Public debt management, as discussed below.
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS

blocks.text: 5.1.  Delay in uploading the Procurement Plan into the IFMIS System by MDAs
heading_path: 5.1.  Delay in uploading the Procurement Plan into the IFMIS System by MDAs

blocks.text: Th e Electronic Government Procurement System (E-GPS) is an end-to-end system that incorporates all procurement processes in line with the Public Procurements and Asset Disposal Act 2015 and its attendant Regulations to be used by all public procuring entities. Th e Implementation of the e-GP system is being carried out in a phased, incremental approach.
heading_path: 5.1.  Delay in uploading the Procurement Plan into the IFMIS System by MDAs

blocks.text: Phase I modules include: Registration (Supplier and Procuring Entity), Annual Procurement and Disposal Plan,  e-requisition,  e-tender  preparation,  e-tender  submission  &  evaluation,  e-tender  award,  e-framework agreement, e-bid security and guarantee management module, e-contract management, and e-Procurement Management Information System, as well as Workflow management. Phase II modules include e-Complaints, e-Compliance, e-Appeals, e-Debarment, Performance Management, Store Management, e-Auctions, e-Catalogues & Marketplace, and e-Reverse Auction.
heading_path: 5.1.  Delay in uploading the Procurement Plan into the IFMIS System by MDAs

blocks.text: Observations
heading_path: Observations

blocks.text: Th e Public Procurement Regulatory Authority issued Circular No.04 2025 Ref: PPRA/6/5 Vol. II(229) dated 12th August 2025 on Enforcement of compliance with the Mandatory use of the Electronic Government Procurement System (E-GPS) by all public procuring entities. Public entities were expected, effective 1st July 2025, to undertake all public procurement and asset disposal transactions through E-GPS.
heading_path: Observations

blocks.text: Analysis of submitted financial and non-financial budget performance reports for the first three months of FY 2025/26 shows that requisition processes through the E-GPS were ongoing, resulting in low budget absorption of funds. Th e e-GPS has posed challenges to the procurement process due to a steep learning curve, integration issues with internal systems, and vendor-related problems that impact efficiency, competitiveness, and timely service delivery.
heading_path: Observations

blocks.text: Recommendation: Accounting  Officers  should  fast-track  the  implementation  of  E-GPS  as  per  the  Circular  by PPRA and in compliance with the Public Procurement and Disposal Act and directives issued by the National Treasury. Th is will enhance transparency, equity, and cost-effectiveness in the use of public resources.
heading_path: Observations

blocks.text: 5.2.  Transition from Cash to Accrual Basis of Accounting
heading_path: 5.2.  Transition from Cash to Accrual Basis of Accounting

blocks.text: Pursuant to the Cabinet approval on 7th March 2024, government entities were to transition from a cash basis to an accrual basis, as subsequently gazetted vide Gazette Notice No. 11033 on 30th August 2024. MDAs adopted a 3-year phased approach to transition, with the first year being 2024/25.
heading_path: 5.2.  Transition from Cash to Accrual Basis of Accounting

blocks.text: MDAs have established committees to spearhead the transition, revised existing accounting policies and manuals, and conducted training for accountants, internal auditors, finance officers, and procurement officers. Th e first transitional statements were prepared and submitted to the Office of the Auditor General by 30th August 2025.
heading_path: 5.2.  Transition from Cash to Accrual Basis of Accounting

blocks.text: Observations:
heading_path: Observations:

blocks.text: Some of the Challenges highlighted by MDAs include: IFMIS is not configured to record accrual transactions and budget execution reported on cash basis even under the accrual reporting framework, entities budgets are prepared and executed on cash basis but FS are prepared on accrual basis thus requiring many reconciliations, Historical assets have not been valued, Challenges in determining fair value of donated assets such as motor vehicles, recognising the fair value of assets.
heading_path: Observations:

blocks.text: Recommendations: For the effective transition and implementation of a Cash to Accrual basis of Accounting, the Controller of Budget recommends continuous training of personnel in IPSAS-compliant recognition and measurement principles, upgrading financial systems to support accrual accounting, and conducting comprehensive asset verification and valuation exercises.
heading_path: Observations:

blocks.text: 5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution
heading_path: 5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya provides for Supplementary appropriation for the national government to spend money that has not been appropriated if the amount appropriated for any purpose under the Appropriation Act is insufficient or a need has arisen for expenditure for a purpose for which no amount has been appropriated by that Act, or money has been withdrawn from the Contingencies Fund. Th e approval of Parliament for any spending under this Article shall be sought within two months a ft er the first withdrawal of the money, subject to clause (3). Clause 5 specifies that in any particular financial year, the national government may not spend under this Article more than ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament for that financial year unless, in special circumstances, Parliament has approved a higher percentage.
heading_path: 5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: In accordance with Regulation 40(3) of the Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulations 2015, the purpose for which approval is sought for supplementary budget shall be Unforeseen and unavoidable, in circumstances where no budget provision was made; or Unavoidable, in circumstances where there is an existing budgetary provision, which is, however, inadequate.
heading_path: 5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: Regulation 40(4) of the Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulation 2015 identifies expenditure that shall not be considered unforeseen and unavoidable. Th is includes expenditure that, although known when finalising the estimates for the original budget, could not be accommodated within allocations, tariff adjustments, and price increases.
heading_path: 5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: Th is reliance on Article 223 to finance foreseeable expenditures contravenes Paragraph 40(4) of the PFM (National Government) Regulations, 2015, highlighting weaknesses in budget planning and the overall reliability of budgeting.
heading_path: 5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: Recommendation: Th e Controller of Budget recommends adopting good planning, budget practices and sound expenditure management by prioritising all essential services and aligning them with operational realities during budget formulation and implementation. In addition, the CS-TNT should expedite the submission of necessary documentation to Parliament for approval within the stipulated two-month period to ensure compliance with constitutional requirements.
heading_path: 5.3.  Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: 5.4.  Public Debt Management
heading_path: 5.4.  Public Debt Management

blocks.text: Article 201 of the Constitution guides all aspects of the principles of public finance in the Republic of Kenya. Article 201 (C) stipulates that the burdens and benefits of the use of resources and public borrowing shall be shared equitably between present and future generations. Th is is further elaborated under Section 15 (c)(d) of the Public Finance Management Act, Cap 412A, 15 (c) over the medium term, the national government's borrowings shall be used only for financing development expenditure and not for recurrent expenditure; 15 (d) public debt and obligations shall be maintained at a sustainable level as approved by Parliament for the national government and the county assembly for county government.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public Debt Management

blocks.text: In FY 2025/26, the national government budget amounts to Kshs.4.69 trillion, comprising Kshs.744.84 billion for ministerial development, Kshs.1.80 trillion for ministerial recurrent and Kshs.2.14 trillion for Consolidated Fund Services expenditure. Allocation to Public Debt amounts to Kshs. 1.90 trillion, representing 41 per cent of the total budget, which is the highest proportion of the annual budget. Ministerial development expenditure recorded 16 per cent of the budget. Debt servicing has reduced the resources available for current spending needs. A significant portion of the government's budget is allocated to debt servicing, leaving less money for other development expenditures. Nonetheless, we commend the government's effort to automate the exchequer process for the national government. Only public-debt-related exchequer processes are yet to be automated.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public Debt Management

blocks.text: Recommendation: To enhance fiscal impact and ensure debt sustainability, borrowing should be strictly aligned with development projects that have measurable economic and social returns. Recurrent expenditure should be contained through expenditure rationalisation and stronger public financial management controls.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public Debt Management

blocks.text: Th e Controller of Budget also recommends full automation and integration of the public debt management system to enhance accuracy and timeliness in data production. All foreign currency-denominated debt is presently being processed manually through the exchequer, whereas other exchequers are automated.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public Debt Management

blocks.text: Further, for effective management of Public Debt, the government should implement comprehensive audits of debt procurement, utilisation, and sustainability. Th is should include auditing the public debt stock, reconciling loan books, and associating loans with specific projects. Th ere should be regular reviews aimed at flagging unsustainable debts to enhance sustainability, transparency and accountability in public borrowing. Th e audit findings should guide future borrowing and repayment strategies and alignment with national development priorities.
heading_path: 5.4.  Public Debt Management

blocks.text: 6. CONCLUSION
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Th e  National  Government  Budget  Implementation  Review  Report  is  published  in  accordance  with  Article 228(6) of the Constitution, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit a report on the implementation of budgets for national and county governments to each House of Parliament every four months. It provides an overview of financial and non-financial information on budget performance for the first three months of FY 2025/26 by analysing receipts into the Consolidated Fund and expenditure against the annual target. It also highlights key issues encountered during the review period and recommends mechanisms for addressing them.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Total receipts into the Consolidated Fund were Kshs.1.03 trillion, representing 23 per cent of the annual target. Th e Controller of Budget approved withdrawals of Kshs.1.02 trillion from the Consolidated Fund, representing 23 per cent of the annual net estimates. Ministries, Departments and Agencies received a Kshs.409.80 billion, representing 22 per cent of the annual net estimates, comprising Kshs.43.31 billion for ministerial development expenditure (11 per cent) and Kshs.366.49 billion for ministerial recurrent expenditure. Consolidated Fund Services received Kshs.546.76 billion, and County Governments received Kshs.66.13 billion as an equitable share of revenues raised nationally, representing 26 per cent and 16 per cent of the annual net estimates, respectively.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Gross expenditure for the National Government was Kshs.1.11 trillion, recording an absorption rate of 24 per cent. Th is  comprised ministerial development expenditure at Kshs.132.65 billion (absorption rate of 18 per cent), ministerial recurrent expenditure at Kshs.433.89 billion (absorption rate of 24 per cent), and Consolidated Fund Services at Kshs.545.48 billion (absorption rate of 25 per cent).
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: In the first three months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that should be addressed for seamless budget implementation. Th ese included the delay in uploading the procurement plan into the IFMIS system by MDAs, the transition from cash to an accrual basis of Accounting, using Article 223 of the Constitution to fund government programmes, and Public debt management.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends that Accounting Officers should fast-track the implementation of E-GPS as per the Circular by PPRA and in compliance with the Public Procurement and Disposal Act and directives issued by the National Treasury. Th is will enhance transparency, equity, and cost-effectiveness in the use of public resources and the absorption of the development budget. For the effective transition and implementation of a Cash to Accrual basis of Accounting, the Controller of Budget recommends continuous training of personnel in IPSAS-compliant recognition and measurement principles, as well as upgrading financial systems to support accrual accounting . To reduce over-reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution on foreseen expenses, it is necessary to adopt good planning and budget practices by prioritising all essential services and aligning them to operational realities during the budget process.   On public debt management, the Controller of Budget recommends that, to enhance fiscal impact and ensure debt sustainability, borrowing should be strictly aligned with development projects that have measurable economic and social returns, full automation and integration of the public debt management system to enhance accuracy and timeliness in data production and the government should implement comprehensive audits of debt procurement, utilisation, and sustainability
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION
